shows.title: Robert Rauschenberg: Important Early Works from the Cy Twombly Foundation
shows.description:
This is a small, tightly focused show built entirely from one collection: six early works by Robert Rauschenberg that Cy Twombly kept for himself. The two artists met in 1951 at the Art Students League, then traveled together through Italy, Morocco, and Spain in the early '50s, and what Twombly held onto over the following decades amounts to a rare, first-hand record of Rauschenberg's formative years — a period when, by his own account, much of his output was lost, destroyed, or cannibalized into later work.

The centerpiece is one of Rauschenberg's earliest surviving sculptures, a 1950 assemblage that would likely not exist today if Twombly hadn't kept it, alongside a life-size cyanotype made with Susan Weil shortly before their marriage, an early Coca-Cola crate assemblage, and a 1952 Black Painting built from oil, newsprint, and gravel. None of this is the Rauschenberg of the Combines or the silkscreens; it's rawer and more provisional, closer to the materials-driven experimentation he and Twombly were doing side by side before either had a settled style.

The show runs alongside Gagosian's Marcel Duchamp exhibition, both timed to the opening of the gallery's new ground-floor space at 980 Madison, and the pairing makes sense: Rauschenberg's readymade-adjacent assemblages from this period owe an obvious debt to Duchamp, filtered through a young artist's very physical, scavenging relationship to materials. For anyone who knows Rauschenberg only through his mature Combines, this is a chance to see where that sensibility actually started.

shows.title: Marcel Duchamp
shows.description:
Gagosian opened its new ground-floor space on Madison Avenue with about as loaded a gesture as the gallery world offers: a room full of Duchamp's readymades. Because the originals were mostly lost or destroyed decades ago, what's on view are the 1964 editions Duchamp made with dealer Arturo Schwarz, including Fountain, Bottle Rack, L.H.O.O.Q., and the Bicycle Wheel, one of the few examples of that piece not already locked away in a museum collection. There's a neat historical hook, too, since these very editions had their American debut just up the block in 1965.

Seeing readymades in a gallery built to sell art has an inherent irony that Duchamp himself would probably have appreciated, given how much of his work was about undermining the idea that authorship and originality make an object precious. The installation gives each piece room to be looked at as a standalone object rather than a punchline, which is a useful corrective for anyone who only knows these works from textbook reproductions.

The show also functions as a quiet victory lap for Larry Gagosian, who has said this building is one he's wanted for years, and it runs concurrently with MoMA's Duchamp retrospective, the artist's first full US museum survey since 1973. Taken together, the two shows make late summer an unusually good moment in New York to reckon with an artist whose ideas about art-as-concept still shape how contemporary art gets made and argued about today.

shows.title: From the Air
shows.description:
Yvonne Jacquette spent decades looking at the world from above — out of airplane windows, from helicopters, from the tops of buildings — and turning that vantage into paintings, pastels, and watercolors that make aerial perspective feel intimate rather than clinical. This survey at Karma's Chelsea space gathers work spanning from the early 1970s watercolors of cloud formations to large late-career oil paintings of highways, paper mills, and city grids seen from a great height.

What's striking across the decades is how consistent her eye stayed even as her subjects changed: a night view of Washington, D.C. and a daylight study of a Maine paper plant are both built from the same fascination with pattern, light, and the strange abstraction that distance imposes on familiar things. Jacquette was associated with a loose circle of New York realists in the 1970s, but her aerial viewpoint set her apart — she found a genuinely new way to paint landscape by refusing to stand on the ground.

The show works well as a chronological record of a single, sustained idea. Early graphite and watercolor studies of clouds and rivers sit alongside the ambitious oil canvases that made her reputation, including sweeping nocturnes of the New York skyline and industrial New England. For anyone who thinks they've seen every possible way to paint a city, this is a reminder that changing your altitude changes everything.

shows.title: Notes from the Margins: Allen Ginsberg and Vivian Maier
shows.description:
Allen Ginsberg and Vivian Maier were born the same year, 1926, and never met, worked in entirely different cities and circles, and are remembered for entirely different things — Ginsberg as the Beat Generation's most visible poet, Maier as a nanny whose 100,000-plus street photographs were discovered only after her death. Pairing them for a joint centennial show is a curatorial gamble that pays off mostly because both bodies of work turn on the same act: pointing a cheap camera at the people and streets immediately around you and trusting that the ordinary will turn out to matter.

Ginsberg's photographs, taken mostly between the early 1950s and 1964 before he lost his camera, are casual, affectionate snapshots of his now-famous circle — Kerouac on a fire escape, Burroughs in Tangier, Neal Cassady checking out used cars — many annotated by hand with Ginsberg's own captions decades later. Maier's pictures, drawn from her vast Chicago-based archive, include a strong run of self-portraits alongside her better-known street work, and the show leans into that self-documenting impulse as a throughline between the two artists.

With around 80 prints, plus Maier's experimental film footage and a recording of Ginsberg reading "Howl," the show is less interested in making a grand formal argument than in letting two very different outsider practices sit in the same room. It works best as a study of the camera as a private tool for self-fashioning — for two people who spent their lives observing everyone around them while remaining, in different ways, hard to fully see themselves.

shows.title: Second Skin
shows.description:
Ryan Wallace's paintings have always been built through accumulation and cutting-apart, and "Second Skin" pushes that process further by cannibalizing his own earlier work. Older paintings get sliced up, their fiberglass substrates, linen, copper, and aluminum layers exposed and recombined so that the back of a piece — the structural scaffolding usually hidden — becomes as much a part of the finished composition as the front.

The result is a body of abstract paintings that read as geological cross-sections as much as pictures: translucent fiberglass sheeting sits over grids of tape lines, sanded passages, and salvaged fragments, with a muted, often monochrome palette of grays, blues, and rusts. The show's title comes from a Chameleons song, and that new-wave, slightly melancholic sensibility runs through the whole installation — surfaces feel worn-in rather than fresh, more like remnants than finished statements.

It's a good entry point for anyone interested in process-based abstraction that's honest about its own materials and history, and a chance to see how far Wallace can stretch a single vocabulary of layering and excavation before it starts to feel like an entirely new language.

shows.title: Continuum
shows.description:
Otis Jones, who died in 2025, spent five decades pushing at the edge where painting turns into object. Continuum gathers ten of his signature wall works, each built from stacked plywood, dripped glue, staples, and heavy layers of pigment that read less as painted surfaces than as excavated ones. Shapes recur across the group — circles, ovals, the ghost of a grid — not as motifs so much as containers for a slow accumulation of gesture, sanded back and rebuilt many times over.

What comes through in these late works is Jones's refusal of speed. His process — paint, sand, scrape, gouge, start again — produced surfaces that feel weathered rather than finished, closer to found objects than studio pictures. The show reads as a fitting summary of an artist who spent his career proving that austerity and reduction could still carry real emotional weight.

For anyone interested in the Texas branch of postwar abstraction, or in what happens to Minimalism when it gets roughed up by hand-labor and time, this small, concentrated exhibition is a chance to spend real time with a body of work that rewards exactly that.

shows.title: OUT OF THE BLUE
shows.artist: Michael Brown, Kiah Celeste, Lucia Hierro, Anna Leonhardt, Moris, Paul Pretzer, Marie Watt, Xi Zhang
shows.description:
OUT OF THE BLUE is a summer group show that uses the color blue as a loose organizing thread across a roster of artists the gallery has worked with for years, rather than as a strict curatorial thesis. It's the kind of show galleries mount in late summer to let a wide range of practices sit side by side — sculpture, textile-based work, painting, and assemblage from Michael Brown, Kiah Celeste, Lucia Hierro, Anna Leonhardt, Moris, Paul Pretzer, Marie Watt, and Xi Zhang.

Given the range of artists involved — from Marie Watt's textile-and-community-based sculpture to Lucia Hierro's soft sculptures riffing on consumer goods to Moris's charged, materially blunt objects — the exhibition works best as a survey of how differently artists working today handle color, material, and scale. It's a low-key, browsable show, useful for viewers who want a quick cross-section of the gallery's program before its fall schedule kicks into gear.

shows.title: Le Sacre Du Printemps
shows.description:
Pierre Knop's third solo show with Yossi Milo is his first devoted entirely to landscape, and the biggest shift is what's missing: the human figure that has anchored his earlier paintings is gone. Eleven new works — built up in oil, acrylic, ink, oil stick, pastel, crayon, and pencil — move through mountains, trees, and water without a single body to orient the viewer, forcing the landscape itself to carry the emotional weight Knop usually assigns to a figure standing in for the viewer's own presence.

The title borrows from Stravinsky's 1913 score, which Knop played on repeat in the studio while making these paintings, and that same interest in dissonance and shifting energy shows up in his process: he builds compositions without a predetermined image, treating mistakes as what he calls "the third hand of painting" and letting accidents redirect each piece. The results sit somewhere between observed landscape and invented memory — recognizable natural forms pushed toward something stranger and more internal.

Knop, who splits his exhibition history between London, Copenhagen, Seoul, and New York, works in a tradition of psychologically-charged landscape painting, and this show is a good test of whether that approach holds up without the figure he's leaned on before.

shows.title: And Yet Again
shows.description:
Katia Santibañez builds her paintings from a rigorously constructed grid, then fills each cell — sometimes as small as half an inch — with a hand-painted spiral or pinwheel motif inspired by forms in nature: snail shells, tree rings, unfurling vines. The tension between that underlying order and the small variations she introduces in color and gesture as she moves across the canvas is the real subject of the work; up close, no two cells are quite identical, even though the overall structure reads as strict and mechanical from a distance.

This show, her latest with DC Moore, brings together new oils on canvas alongside gouaches and works on paper, continuing an approach to the grid that Santibañez has developed since 2007. It's patient, meditative work that asks for the same close, sustained looking it took to make — paintings built to reward the kind of slow attention that feels increasingly rare.

The show runs concurrently with the gallery's group exhibition On, In, Off the Grid, which puts Santibañez's systematic abstraction in dialogue with other artists working through related structural logics.

shows.title: On, In, Off the Grid
shows.description:
A tightly focused group show built around a single organizing idea: the grid as a generative structure rather than a rigid constraint. Joell Baxter, Lisa Corinne Davis, Valerie Jaudon, Alfred Jensen, Richard Kalina, Holly Miller, Stephen Mueller, Leslie Roberts, James Siena, Stanley Whitney, and George Woodman all appear here, spanning decades and wildly different formal languages — from Jaudon's crisp, decorative pattern paintings to Siena's obsessively worked graphite grids to Whitney's saturated stacked color fields.

What ties the work together is process: each artist develops a systematic, often self-imposed method — a repeated interval, a fixed unit, a modular color logic — and then either follows it faithfully or deliberately breaks it to generate new possibilities. Seen together, the works make a quiet case for the grid as one of postwar abstraction's most durable and flexible tools, equally capable of imposing calm order or engineering visual disruption.

The show runs alongside Katia Santibañez's solo exhibition And Yet Again at the same gallery, extending its own grid-based logic into a full room of related company.

shows.title: Certainly an Act: Works on Paper by Pope.L
shows.description:
This survey pulls together more than two hundred works on paper by Pope.L (1955–2023), an artist better known for grueling endurance performances like The Great White Way than for drawing — and makes the case that drawing was, in fact, the connective tissue running through everything he did. The show spans five decades and includes the long-running Skin Set series, in which caricatured faces and deadpan capitalized text ("BLACK PEOPLE ARE WHAT BLACK PEOPLE LACK") turn racial categories into absurdist, self-undermining slogans, alongside Failure Drawings and a rarely-shown installation piece, Relational Painting a.k.a If Black Is Beautiful.

What comes through across the sprawl of material — drawings, drawing-based films, writings, audio pieces — is Pope.L's insistence that a mark on paper is never neutral: it's an event, an act with consequences, whether it's a caricature, a brand name repurposed to unsettle, or a smear of peanut butter standing in for the body. Humor is the delivery system for a relentless interrogation of how race, language, and power get constructed and reproduced.

For anyone who knows Pope.L mainly through the crawl performances or the Skin Set text works alone, this exhibition is a chance to see how deep and formally varied his works-on-paper practice actually was — proof that even his most conceptual gestures started, literally, with a line.

shows.title: Drawing Connections: Student Exhibition
shows.description:
A showcase of work made by New York City elementary and high school students in The Drawing Center's Michael Iovenko School Programs — Drawing Connections and Drawing All-Stars with Teen Art Salon. Students from P.S. 42, Lexington School for the Deaf, Chelsea CTE High School, and a cohort of citywide Van Lier Fellows produced work in direct response to the institution's own recent exhibitions, using drawing as a tool to think through ideas rather than simply illustrate them.

It's a modest, unglamorous show by design, but it's also a useful reminder of what a kunsthalle like this one does beyond mounting museum-caliber exhibitions: it runs a genuine pipeline of arts education, and this room is where that work gets to hang on the same walls as the professionals.

shows.title: Lightscape
shows.description:
Doug Aitken has spent decades treating landscape as an active collaborator rather than passive backdrop, and Lightscape is his most ambitious attempt yet to turn that idea into a full-body theatrical experience. Installed across seven screens filling a 12,000-square-foot gallery at The Shed, the roughly hour-long piece was originally conceived as a live symphonic event with the LA Philharmonic before being reworked into this standalone cinematic installation, featuring contributions from an unusually stacked group of collaborators spanning film, dance, and music.

The piece uses Los Angeles, and the sprawl and diversity of American urban life more broadly, as its real subject, weaving footage into something closer to a mood piece than a conventional narrative. Actress Natasha Lyonne anchors the human element, while music from Philip Glass, Beck, Gustavo Dudamel, and Steve Reich, along with movement from members of the L.A. Dance Project, gives the installation an unusually layered soundtrack for a visual-art piece. The Shed has also scheduled live performances tied to the run, underscoring that this is meant to function as much as a venue for events as a fixed installation.

For anyone who thinks of Aitken mainly through his earlier film and sculpture work, Lightscape is a chance to see him working at a genuinely large scale, with the resources of an institution built for exactly this kind of hybrid, multi-screen spectacle. It's an immersive, sensory show more than an analytical one, and worth planning around given its run ends in mid-September.

shows.title: Whitney Biennial 2026
shows.description:
Now in its eighty-second edition, the Whitney Biennial remains the museum's marquee statement on where American art stands at this exact moment, and this year's version leans into mood and feeling rather than tidy thesis statements. Fifty-six artists, duos, and collectives fill the building, with work spanning painting, sculpture, video, textiles, and installation, including pieces by artists based well outside the mainland US, in places shaped by the long reach of American power. The result is less a survey with a single argument than a chorus of different, sometimes contradictory, positions on identity, geopolitics, and belonging.

By late August the run has become a moving target: the fifth-floor galleries already closed, the first-floor presentation wraps up in early September, and only the sixth floor stays on view through mid-October, so this is very much a show to catch on a deadline. Expect an eclectic physical experience, too, from scaffolding hung with photographs to circular platforms crowded with small figurines and a room-filling inflatable jester. A billboard component across from the Museum's Gansevoort Street entrance extends the exhibition beyond the galleries themselves.

Whatever your take on biennial-format shows in general, this one is worth seeing simply because it functions as a snapshot of the art conversation happening right now, curated by a team led by Marcela Guerrero and Drew Sawyer. It rewards visitors willing to wander without a fixed narrative and let the accumulation of small, strange, and pointed gestures add up on their own terms.

shows.title: On the other hand
shows.description:
Margot Bergman's fifth solo show in New York is built around a pivot point in her own practice. For roughly fifteen years she made her uncanny portraits by painting into existing, anonymous canvases bought at Chicago thrift stores — coaxing faces out of landscapes and still lifes by turning a clearing in the woods into a head or a vase into an eye. In 2012 she set that method aside for blank canvases, and this show reunites paintings from that transitional period (2012–14) with the large-scale invented portraits that followed (2015–19), most never shown together in New York before.

What connects the two groups is a kind of jazz-inflected improvisation: meandering lines plotted like slurred notes, repeated motifs, and a vocabulary of flowers, horizon lines, and lattice patterns lifted from her studio in the woods. The later portraits push further into a raw, unfinished-looking style — photorealistic eyes next to scribbled hair, thin color washes over bare canvas — that has more in common with Dada collage than with conventional portraiture. Nothing here is resolved or polished; Bergman treats every irregularity as material rather than mistake.

It's a useful show for anyone who knows Bergman only through the found-painting works, since it makes the case that the freedom of the blank canvas didn't erase her earlier method so much as free it to become stranger. The late works on view, including 2019's Pupa, show faces dissolving back into pattern — a full-circle gesture from an artist still finding new ways to unmake and remake the same idea of a face.

shows.title: Booty
shows.description:
Marcus Jahmal's third solo show with Anton Kern takes pirates as its subject — not the historical record of transatlantic plunder and slavery, but the swashbuckling, Treasure Island version that popular culture has turned into a symbol of outlaw freedom. Jahmal paints his buccaneers with the warped, elongated anatomy that's become his signature: peg legs, hook hands, and wide-brimmed hats rendered against flat, saturated grounds, with contemporary details like bandanas and jeans breaking the historical costume and reminding you these are actors playing a part rather than portraits of anyone real.

The show's title plays a double game, referring both to plundered treasure and to the body as an object of desire — a slippage Jahmal makes literal with piles of Swarovski crystals heaped on the gallery floor, sculptural stand-ins for loot waiting to be taken. It's a way of holding two things at once: the swagger and theater of pirate mythology, and the violent colonial history that mythology tends to launder out of the picture.

Coming right after Jahmal co-curated the gallery's group show GIVE ME TWO earlier this year, Booty finds him back in a purely painterly mode, using an absurdist, pop-inflected register to smuggle in a harder historical argument.

shows.title: NY Window
shows.description:
Alessandro Pessoli's first show at Anton Kern's storefront project space WINDOW is an exercise in density: 57 works on paper installed floor-to-ceiling, wrapping entirely around the interior of the small street-level window on Walker Street. Visible around the clock from the sidewalk, it functions almost like a single sprawling mural made of individual sheets rather than a conventional hang.

Pessoli's drawings work in vignettes rather than a single continuous story — fragments of Americana, religious iconography, pop culture, and everyday incident, with figures and animals caught between euphoria and violence, boredom and temptation. Nothing resolves into a clean narrative; instead the accumulation of scenes, seen all together through glass, adds up to a scattered, slightly anxious portrait of ordinary life's absurdities. It's Pessoli's ninth show with the gallery but his first at WINDOW, and the space's constraints — no door, no controlled lighting, viewable only from outside — suit his loose, diaristic mark-making better than a white cube might.

venue.name: Anton Kern Gallery — WINDOW
venue.address_detail: corner of Walker and Lafayette Street
hours: Open 24 hours, viewable from the street

shows.title: Deana Lawson
shows.description:
Deana Lawson's first solo exhibition with Gagosian debuts new work from Edge Control, a series she began in 2023 that reworks the surveillance stills taped up in beauty supply stores across the United States. Lawson has always built her elaborately staged portraits around questions of Black interiority and self-presentation; here she turns to found rather than staged imagery, appropriating the grainy, deep-blue-and-green footage that stores use to catch shoplifters and reframing it as a kind of accidental portraiture.

The title refers to the styling gel that's reportedly one of the most frequently stolen items in these stores — a product used to smooth hairlines into a polished look — and Lawson plays that literal meaning against the broader idea of "edge control" as a metaphor for surveillance and the policing of Black bodies and behavior. She frames the images in luminous black mirrors, a device that turns the act of looking at the photograph into an act of seeing yourself look, and that gestures toward the images' strange, secondhand futurity.

It's a departure in method from the tableau photography Lawson is best known for, but consistent with her longstanding interest in how images of Black life get made, controlled, and circulated by systems the subjects don't control — and in what happens when an artist intervenes to reclaim them.

shows.title: I Am Plane Image
shows.description:
Organized with Brice Marden's estate and timed to a new catalogue raisonné of his paintings, this is the first comprehensive Marden survey to appear in New York in twenty years — six decades of work, from a 1966 painting inspired by a cross-country road trip through Nebraska (which Marden kept and hung in his own home for the rest of his life) up through late works from the 2010s. Loans from the Art Institute of Chicago, the Whitney, and major private collections fill out a show whose ambition is closer to a museum retrospective than a typical gallery exhibition.

Marden's own description of his project — "tightening the relationship of the image to the plane" — is a useful way into the show's arc: from the near-monochrome, beeswax-thickened panels he developed after immersing himself in New York's downtown scene in the mid-1960s, through the brighter palette that emerged once he began spending summers on the Greek island of Hydra, to the calligraphic, looping line paintings of his final decades. Seeing the early flat panels next to the later linear work makes clear how much ground he covered while staying loyal to a single, almost austere question about what a painted surface can hold.

For a painter this influential, actual opportunities to see the full sweep of his career in one room are rare, and this show — arriving posthumously, with the artist's estate's full cooperation — is likely to be the definitive New York account of his work for some time.

shows.title: Cristina BanBan: Jaque Mate
shows.description:
Cristina BanBan returns to Skarstedt's Upper East Side space with a new body of oil paintings built around the tangle of bodies she's become known for — figures pressed together, limbs overlapping, flesh rendered in thick, confident strokes that owe as much to Lucian Freud's physicality as to Latin American figurative painting. The title, Spanish for "checkmate," hints at the charged, strategic quality of the encounters she paints: intimacy as a contest of positions.

The canvases on view, all made this year, share a scale (76 x 56 inches) that puts the viewer at close range with monumental, entangled nudes. BanBan has spent the last several years refining a vocabulary of distended anatomy and compressed space, and this show reads as a concentrated, single-room statement of where that vocabulary now stands — heavier on ambiguity, looser in the paint handling, less interested in individual likeness than in the collective mass of bodies in contact.

It's a tightly focused gallery show rather than a survey, which suits the work: BanBan's paintings reward the kind of sustained, close looking that a small selection of large canvases makes possible.

shows.title: Danh Vo
shows.description:
Danh Vo's return to New York arrives eight years after his Guggenheim survey "Take My Breath Away," and follows directly from a major museum presentation at the Stedelijk Amsterdam earlier this year built around fragments of antiquities, religious relics, and monument pieces. That same working method — taking apart historical and devotional objects and reassembling their pieces into new, unstable wholes — is the throughline of Vo's practice, and it's a safe bet this White Cube presentation continues to mine it.

Vo has long worked at the boundary between personal history and colonial history: his family's flight from Vietnam, Catholic iconography, American military memorabilia, and classical statuary have all passed through his hands and come out reconfigured, often literally cut apart and rejoined. The result is sculpture that behaves like evidence — fragments that ask you to reconstruct a narrative the artist has deliberately left incomplete.

Showing in the gallery's Madison Avenue townhouse rather than a larger industrial space, this exhibition should reward close, patient looking at a scale closer to the intimacy of relics than the spectacle of installation art — fitting for an artist whose central subject is what survives, and in what condition, when things are moved across distance and time.

shows.title: Inevitable, inveterate
shows.artist: Tomoko Amaki Abe, Susan Bee, Liz Surbeck Biddle, Sasha Chavchavadze, Yvette Drury Dubinsky, Maxine Henryson, Zini Lardieri, Xanda McCagg, Sylvia Netzer, Ann Schaumburger, Kathleen Schneider, Joan Snitzer, Erica Stoller, Nancy Storrow
shows.description:
Fourteen members of A.I.R. Gallery come together for this group exhibition, whose title borrows a slip of the pen from a letter between founding member Rosemary Mayer and her sister, the poet Bernadette Mayer. That accidental phrase — "inevitable, I mean inveterate worker" — becomes a lens for looking at the compulsion to make art as something both automatic and hard-won.

The works on view range widely in material and approach, from dead leaves and cactus roots to repurposed cardboard, reflecting the cooperative's long-standing ethos that feminist art is defined less by a single style than by a shared practice of mutual support among women artists. Curators Taylor Bluestine and Audrey Min have organized the show as a kind of correspondence among the participating artists, echoing the epistolary exchange that inspired its title.

As a survey of current work by longtime A.I.R. members, the show offers a useful entry point into the country's longest-running alternative space for women and non-binary artists, now approaching its move from Brooklyn back to Manhattan. It's a modest but rewarding chance to see how a founding feminist principle — art made through collectivity rather than in isolation — still plays out across fourteen very different studios.

shows.title: La Cosecha (The Harvest)
shows.description:
Romina Chuls's first New York solo show takes a 1,700-year-old Nasca textile — now in the Brooklyn Museum's collection — as a springboard for a body of knitted and ceramic work about fertility, grief, and care. The original mantle, found wrapped around a body buried in fetal position, depicted a harvest procession; Chuls reworks its iconography into forms that read as much medical as agricultural, threading in allusions to reproductive technology alongside the textile's ancient imagery.

Pieces like the large knitted hanging Eucaristía use steamed common rue, ceramic, and aluminum rod to suggest anatomy as much as pattern — vase-like appendages, knitted petals, and latex hoses stained with iron oxide recur throughout the installation. The effect lands somewhere between reliquary and clinic, treating gestation, miscarriage, and abortion as points on the same continuous cycle rather than as opposites.

Chuls is a recipient of A.I.R.'s 2025–2026 Fellowship, and the show reflects the kind of first-solo-in-New-York opportunity that program is built to provide. It's a quiet, materially rich exhibition that rewards close looking at the handwork itself as much as at its conceptual scaffolding.

shows.title: between the skin and flesh, a thing
shows.description:
Mae Howard's inaugural solo show centers on a series of transparent leather hides printed with photographs documenting BDSM scenes in which Howard is both subject and co-author. Made in collaboration with a group of leather practitioners over five years, the works use sutures, scalpels, and other tools borrowed from medical contexts as instruments of authorship, deliberately diffusing the idea of a single artist behind the images.

The photographic prints on hide carry an unusual physicality — the printing process leaves a veined texture across the leather's grain, so the images read as embedded in the material rather than sitting on its surface. Howard's work draws on their long engagement with disability, endurance, and leather history, framing pain and pleasure as sites of collective, rather than purely individual, experience.

It's an intense, unapologetically corporeal show, accompanied by a room-filling scent commissioned from agustine zegers, and one of the more distinctive solo debuts in this fall's crop of gallery openings.

shows.title: Field Conditions
shows.description:
Soumya Netrabile's second solo show at Anat Ebgi pairs new oil paintings with glazed terra cotta sculptures, both built from the same vocabulary of rounded, accumulating forms. The title borrows a term from meteorology and construction reporting — language used to describe how physical conditions affect a site or a game — and applies it to the studio, where mood, weather, and unpredictable daily pressures shape what ends up on the canvas.

In paintings like The Moss Fields and Evening Caucus, tangled brushwork and bulbous, interlocking shapes sit against banded, atmospheric grounds, compressing pictorial space into something that feels more like a living system than a landscape. The ceramic works extend the same logic into three dimensions, folding tubular and ribbon-like forms into asymmetrical mounds where pooled glazes trace the seams and ridges left by hand-modeling.

Netrabile, who trained as an electrical engineer before turning to painting, has exhibited widely from Chicago to London to Seoul, and her work sits in public collections including the Orange County Museum of Art and the Crocker Art Museum. This show finds her pushing the same intuitive, materials-led process across two mediums at once, each informing the other's sense of structure and surface.

shows.title: Solastalgia
shows.description:
Alannah Farrell's third solo show with Anat Ebgi takes its title from a term coined by philosopher Glenn Albrecht for the grief of watching a home environment change beyond recognition. Farrell applies it to the rural Southern Tier region of New York where they grew up, painting decaying architecture, shuttered storefronts, and empty parking lots alongside the tender portraits they're best known for.

The paintings are all worked from life, and that commitment shows in how specifically observed the settings are — a condemned school auditorium seen through a shattered window, a nude figure crouched in a bathtub surrounded by houseplants in a portrait titled for a local antique shop. Influences from George Tooker's uncanny realism and Pierre Molinier's staged eroticism surface in the psychodramatic, near-cinematic quality of scenes like Surrender and Longing, where two nude figures entangle at a train crossing under a hazy sunset.

Farrell, a Cooper Union graduate whose work is in the permanent collection of Miami's Institute of Contemporary Art, uses a heightened palette of greens, reds, and oranges to turn ordinary rural decay into something closer to an elegy — a community observed with real intimacy right as it slips away.

shows.title: Conduits of the Unseen: Women Artists Imagine Other Worlds
shows.description:
Curated by Bard College art historian Susan L. Aberth, this group show gathers seventeen women artists from the early twentieth century onward who tried to give visual form to spirits, cosmic forces, and other planes of consciousness. The anchor is Paulina Peavy, a self-taught visionary painter who claimed her paintings, drawings, and masks were channeled through a spirit guide named Lacamo over the course of five decades — the exhibition follows the 2023 publication of the first monograph on her work.

Around Peavy, the show builds out a genealogy of mediumistic and esoteric art-making: Agatha Wojciechowsky's ink drawings recording a language she said came through spiritual contact, Agnes Pelton's semi-abstract paintings drawn from meditation and Theosophy, Hilla Rebay's abstract watercolors, and Surrealists Leonora Carrington and Leonor Fini, whose work approached the unseen through myth and psychodrama rather than active channeling. Also on view are lesser-known figures like Adele Watson, Juanita Guccione, Marjorie Cameron, and Sylvia Fein, each arriving at visionary territory by a different route — Theosophy, Surrealism, occult study, or personal cosmology.

What ties the show together isn't style but intent: all seventeen artists treated painting and drawing as a way of making the invisible legible, whether that meant a literal spirit world or an inner one. It's a rare chance to see channeled, occult, and outsider-adjacent work by women placed in direct dialogue with recognized Surrealist names, in a show that argues they were doing fundamentally related work all along.

shows.title: Weaving a Day, Mourning a Life: The Mother and Daughter-in-Law of Phúc Sen
shows.artist: Trung Duc Nguyen, Minh Sang Chu, Chu Thieu, Trà My Phan
shows.description:
Curated by Dala Nguyen as apexart's fall Open Call winner, this group show translates a specific Northern Vietnamese mourning custom into a three-part installation. In the village of Phúc Sen, a mother-in-law and daughter-in-law weave daily on separate looms; when the elder dies, the accumulated cloth becomes her funeral garment, later dyed indigo and returned to daily wear — grief materially recycled into continued life.

The exhibition builds that idea out across disciplines: large-format photographs by Trung Duc Nguyen document the weaving process and the transformed garment in daily use; a multi-channel sound installation by Minh Sang Chu weaves together loom rhythms, village ambience, and fragments of oral history; and a suspended textile sculpture by Trà My Phan, made from indigo-dyed and undyed handwoven cloth alongside raw cotton, gives the show's central metaphor physical form. A two-channel video by Chu Thieu and Minh Sang Chu adds a further layer of parallel, durational labor.

It's a modest but conceptually tight show, more ethnographic meditation than spectacle, and true to apexart's mission of foregrounding curatorial ideas over marquee names — an original way of thinking about mourning, women's labor, and material continuity through a tradition most New York visitors will be encountering for the first time.

shows.title: Multiple Offerings
shows.description:
This is the first retrospective in twenty-five years devoted to Theresa Hak Kyung Cha, an artist and writer whose career was cut brutally short in 1982, when she was murdered in New York just weeks before what was to be her exhibition at this same institution. Organized by BAMPFA and curated by Victoria Sung with Tausif Noor, the show fills Artists Space's entire first floor with performance-based film and video, installation, photography, artist's books, and works on paper, drawn from the archive Cha's family gave to BAMPFA in 1992.

Cha worked across disciplines with a consistent interest in how language, image, and sound generate meaning only through active interpretation — what she called "Multiple Telling with Multiple Offering." That framework structures the show itself, which is organized around recurring themes of memory, displacement, and linguistic instability rather than strict chronology. Highlights include the 16mm film Permutations and documentation of her performance work, alongside the unfinished black-and-white photographic series she was making from her day job at the Met's European Sculpture and Decorative Arts Department at the time of her death.

Best known for her 1982 book Dictée, a genre-defying collage of poetry, found text, and image, Cha has become an increasingly influential reference point for artists working with language and diaspora — she appeared in the 2022 Whitney Biennial and the 2022 Hessel Museum retrospective. Seeing this much of her archival material together, in the city where her final chapter was cut short, gives the show real historical weight beyond its scholarly ambitions.

shows.title: Noces
shows.description:
Christine Safa's paintings work from a place of hard-won calm — the Beirut-born, Paris-based artist has written about hearing echoes of wartime planes in the ordinary aircraft noise over her current home, and about consciously choosing to notice what light picks out instead. Noces gathers new canvases built from that discipline: birds, rooftops read as mountains, treelines standing in for a horizon, a sun that becomes a moon as it moves.

Works like La convalescence show Safa's touch for layering thin, atmospheric passages of oil paint into scenes that hover between observed landscape and interior state, resisting a clean read as either. The paintings don't resolve their tension between fear and peace so much as hold both in suspension, which gives even her quietest compositions a charge.

This is a small, tightly focused presentation — Safa's poetic writing accompanying the show underscores how personal the material is, closer to a private diary of noticing than a grand painterly statement, and it rewards a slow look accordingly.

shows.title: Daniel Buren & Barbara Kasten
shows.description:
This two-person show pairs a pioneer of institutional critique with a photographer who spent her career interrogating the same questions of structure and perception through a different medium. Daniel Buren has built a five-decade practice around his signature 8.7cm stripe, using it as a tool to expose the architecture and conventions of the spaces where art is shown — his "situated works" are made in direct response to the site itself. Barbara Kasten's photographs and constructed light installations, meanwhile, treat geometric forms, mirrors, and colored gels as a way of making the photographic apparatus and physical space equally visible.

Shown together, the two make a compelling case that photography and installation-based conceptual art were pursuing related ends: both artists strip away illusionism to foreground the literal conditions of seeing — light, surface, structure, and the room itself as the actual subject.

Presented at Bortolami's 55 Walker Street space, the show is a useful pairing of a canonical European conceptualist with an American photographer whose reputation has grown substantially in recent years, placing two very different but complementary formal vocabularies in the same rooms.

shows.title: Yuan Yuan
shows.description:
Shanghai-born, Berlin-based painter Yuan Yuan is known for meticulously rendered interiors of abandoned or decaying grand spaces — crumbling ballrooms, overgrown palace rooms, water-damaged theaters — painted with a photorealist's precision but composited from imagined or hybrid architecture rather than any single real site. The effect is uncanny: rooms that feel historically specific and utterly plausible but exist nowhere, saturated with a sense of accumulated time and abandonment.

This presentation, staged in the Upstairs space at 39 Walker Street, continues that project, most likely showing new large-scale canvases that layer architectural ornament, water stains, and overgrowth into dense, atmospheric scenes. Yuan's work sits at an interesting crossroads of Old Master painting technique and a distinctly contemporary interest in ruin and entropy — spaces that look grand and forgotten at once.

It's a good complement to the ground-floor and 55 Walker shows running concurrently, rounding out a Bortolami season built around artists who use extreme technical control to investigate structure, surface, and the passage of time.

shows.title: Primo Piano
shows.description:
Claire Oswalt's work has long lived at the intersection of painting and sewing — cut and stitched swaths of pigmented canvas reassembled into asymmetrical, landscape-inflected compositions where the seams and stretched edges do as much formal work as the color itself. Primo Piano, Italian for "first floor" or "main floor," suggests a return to fundamentals, and based on the artist's recent output that likely means a continued exploration of her signature wrapped-edge stretchers and sewn color fields.

Oswalt, who splits her time between Austin and Southampton, builds her paintings from breezy, layered passages of pigment that reference landscape without depicting it literally, letting cut and re-stitched canvas create an inbuilt framing device that plays with illusionistic depth. Her work reads as painterly abstraction with a distinctly tactile, almost garment-like construction process behind it.

This marks Oswalt's fourth show with Broadway since her 2021 New York solo debut at the gallery, and it continues a body of work that consistently finds new formal possibilities in the basic act of cutting and sewing paint-soaked cloth.

shows.title: The World Is Not Enough
shows.description:
Libby Rothfeld's third solo show at Bureau continues her interest in the sculptural residue of institutional authority and consumer desire, working in the space between readymade and hand-fabricated object. Rothfeld, who lives and works in Queens, has built a practice around wry, materially specific sculpture that borrows the visual language of retail display, bureaucratic furniture, and domestic clutter to needle at questions of status and want.

Titled after a Bond film but pointed squarely at the everyday, the show's title suggests an appetite that outruns whatever's on offer — a fitting frame for Rothfeld's work, which often takes the form of near-functional objects (dashboards, dividers, display fixtures) pushed slightly out of true. Her sculptures tend to reward close inspection of surface and material choice as much as any conceptual punchline.

Rothfeld's recent survey Selects: Libby Rothfeld, 2016-2024 at Illinois State University gave a sense of how consistent this vein of inquiry has been across a decade of work; this new show extends it with material made specifically for Bureau's Tribeca space.

shows.title: As It Happens
shows.description:
Presented on Bureau's lower level, Will Yackulic's new paintings are small-scale, direct-observation studies built on birch panels — a format he's worked in for five years, one that allows for quick execution and, just as often, quick destruction; by his own account he's scraped down and painted over as many panels as he's exhibited. That churn shows through in works like Queens and In the Pines II, where earlier images bleed through beneath layers of shimmer and haze.

The subjects are deliberately unglamorous and specific: a baseball pitcher cropped from a fan's snapshot, hazy under-bridge traffic pulled from a decade-old Super 8 reel, a squash sitting on a book on the artist's desk. Painted in a uniformly vertical format that invites a portrait-like reading even when the "sitter" is an object or a stranger glimpsed from a distance, the works move between obsessive surface detail and loose, atmospheric mark-making depending on what each image seems to need.

There's a diaristic quality to the show, less about narrative than about the accumulated texture of paying close attention to ordinary things over time — small, quietly funny paintings that reward the same patience it took to make them.

shows.title: Ideas (cont.)
shows.description:
Scott Reeder's second solo show at CANADA gathers a loose family of paintings that treat "ideas" themselves as a subject worth needling. Skeletons and dogs stand in for people going about ordinary business — lounging poolside, staring at screens — rendered with the loose, candy-lit brushwork that recalls Bonnard as much as it does Matisse, whose 1940 interior Reeder directly quotes in one canvas. Alongside the figurative works are Reeder's signature "list paintings," deadpan conceptual pieces that stack handwritten text — to-do lists, plant names, non-sequiturs — into compositions that ask whether language can do a painting's job as well as image can.

The show's real throughline isn't any single motif but Reeder's restless switching between modes: figuration, text-based conceptualism, and loose abstraction all appear side by side, each treated with the same wry, unforced humor. It's a body of work that trusts absurdity as a serious method, in the tradition of Magritte's late, cartoon-derived Vache paintings, and it rewards viewers willing to take a joke as seriously as a brushstroke.

shows.title: Slurpee Machine
shows.description:
In CANADA's project room, Tyson Reeder presents a candy-colored suite of paintings and note-card drawings that read like transmissions from an imaginary nightclub — part Weimar cabaret, part sixties happening, part discotheque adrift in space. Figures in spandex bodysuits pose and play instruments while cars streak through neon coral reefs and escalators climb through abandoned malls, all rendered with a magpie's approach to material: nail polish, glitter, thumbprints, and the printed texture of corrugated cardboard all turn up on the same surface.

The paintings owe a debt to Pattern and Decoration's love of ornament and to the kitsch-embracing irreverence of Sigmar Polke, but the note-card drawings are the real key to the show — loose, immediate, made anywhere and for no one in particular, they're the raw material Reeder's larger paintings grow out of. Together the two bodies of work make the case that a voracious, anything-goes drawing practice is what keeps his painting loose and alive.

shows.title: Landmarks
shows.description:
Alix Vernet's Landmarks turns the gallery into a study of memory made physical — objects and images standing in for places and moments that have otherwise disappeared. Vernet works in a quiet, materially inventive vocabulary of cast and constructed forms, treating the gallery itself as a kind of map of recollection, where each piece marks a coordinate rather than illustrates a scene.

The show continues Vernet's interest in how personal history gets encoded into everyday objects — a rear-view mirror, a fragment of architecture — asking what it means to landmark an experience rather than simply depict it. It's a subtle, deliberately unshowy body of work that asks for a slow look.

shows.title: All of My Angels Wear a Rag: I The Tuner
shows.description:
Presented in Chapter NY's side room, Giuseppe Francalanza's All of My Angels Wear a Rag: I The Tuner is the first chapter of a longer, serially-titled project — a hint that the artist is building a mythology in installments rather than delivering a single self-contained statement. The work leans into raw, tactile materials and a private, incantatory language of titles that reads more like liturgy than exhibition text.

Shown alongside Alix Vernet's Landmarks in the gallery's main space, Francalanza's contribution offers a rougher, more intuitive counterpoint — a smaller-scale, closer-quarters encounter with an artist still early in unpacking a bigger body of ideas.
