shows.title: Alice in the Land of Violence
shows.description:
This show gathers Valerio Adami's paintings and drawings from 1962–1967, a raw, transitional stretch before he settled into the crisp, black-outlined "cloisonné" style he's known for. The works on view — hotel rooms, automobiles, fragmented interiors — sit closer to Surrealism and early Pop than to the graphic hard edges of his mature paintings, made in the years just after Adami left Milan for Paris and fell in with Roberto Matta, Wifredo Lam, and a circle of writers that included Octavio Paz and Jacques Derrida.

Cars and hotel rooms recur throughout as twin obsessions: the car as a symbol of speed, freedom, and mechanical desire (Adami enrolled in a high-speed driving school in 1963), the hotel room as a site of anonymity and psychological compression, the "studio of convenience" for an artist who painted his way through the Chelsea Hotel and befriended Allen Ginsberg on his first trip to New York. The exhibition marks Adami's first appearance in the city in nearly twenty-five years.

Beyond the biographical interest, what's most striking here is watching a vocabulary get built in real time — the flat color fields and hard black contours that would define Adami's signature style are visibly forming, still loose, still argued with, not yet locked into place. For anyone who knows only the later, more polished Adami, this is a chance to see the messier, more searching work that got him there.

shows.title: If Blue is a Holy Color
shows.description:
Julia Bland's third solo show at Derek Eller brings together textile-painting hybrids and hanging sculptures built through weaving, dyeing, braiding, embroidering, and painting — a process that treats fabric the way a painter treats pigment. Pastel ginigham-like weaves sit next to graphic candy-stripe canvas, and out of that assembled, half-order/half-chaos surface, symbols recur: ladders, stars, boats, references that reach toward Jewish iconography and the idea of transcendence (Jacob's ladder chief among them).

An 8mm film included in the show extends Bland's interest in weaving as a way of thinking about time — the steady back-and-forth of warp and weft standing in for the eternal and the earthly measures we use to track duration. Bland's hanging ladder-form sculptures are the show's most literal expression of this: structures that are at once carriers, protectors, and metaphors for escape.

Bland works out of Brooklyn and has shown at the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum, the Everson Museum, and in group shows internationally; this is a body of work that rewards close, slow looking at how a woven surface can hold as much meaning as a painted one.

shows.title: Curtsy
shows.description:
In Derek Eller's North Room, Antone Könst makes his first solo appearance at the gallery with a series of paintings built around a single gesture: the curtsy. Figures hover mid-motion, arms outstretched, gazes ambiguous — caught between deference and defiance, formality and unraveling. Könst treats the pose less as a subject to depict than as a structure to think with, letting dresses become stages for color, pattern, and symbolic play.

Könst has described his own paintings as "Rube Goldberg machines" — accumulations of gesture and incident that snap into legibility almost by accident. That improvisational logic is on full display here: garments read alternately as fire, pearls, or pure abstraction, and the paintings balance a loose, quick touch against careful, deliberate structure.

A CalArts and Yale MFA graduate now based in Brooklyn, Könst has shown at Marianne Boesky, Tilton Gallery, and CASTLE in Los Angeles; this is his gallery debut with Derek Eller.

shows.title: American Traditional
shows.description:
Cannupa Hanska Luger inaugurates Garth Greenan's new 10 Greene Street space with a suite of matte-black sculptures that read like relics dredged up from a mournful, unresolved history. Working in ironstone clay finished with sumi ink and direct flame, Luger builds a monochrome world where Buffalo nickels, Pulaski axes, railroad spikes, and concertina wire are arranged alongside ceramic replicas of a skinned bison, stacked bison skulls, and a severed rifle — all sitting atop a burned, bone-black "American Traditional" style dining table.

The show's centerpiece, a life-size skinned bison built with a hand-embroidery technique Luger developed specifically for the piece, updates his 2020 work (No)stalgia into something even more elegiac. The uniform black finish strips away the bright, declarative color that usually defines Luger's practice, replacing it with a hush that makes the violence of westward expansion — and the selective, mutable nature of how that history gets remembered — feel closer to a funeral than a monument.

Luger, an enrolled member of the Three Affiliated Tribes of the Fort Berthold Reservation, is best known for the Mirror Shield Project he initiated in support of Standing Rock's Water Protectors; this show arrives on the tenth anniversary of that project, adding a darker, more interior register to a practice usually associated with collective action.

shows.title: My Life Has a Life of Its Own
shows.description:
Garth Greenan inaugurates its new 25 Greene Street space with a major survey of Rosalyn Drexler's landmark 1960s Pop paintings — the artist's fifth show with the gallery, and her first since her death last year at 98. Drexler was appropriating tabloid and pulp imagery into overpainted collage-paintings at the same moment Warhol and Lichtenstein were, but has only recently begun receiving comparable critical recognition; this show, curated by Fiona Laugharn, is a corrective.

Organized in three sections — "The Image," "Image and Text," and "Return to Image" — the exhibition pairs iconic paintings like Kiss Me Stupid and F.B.I. with newly surfaced source photographs, sketchbooks, and journals, tracing exactly how Drexler cut, layered, and repainted found imagery into her own sinister, deadpan register. The result is less a greatest-hits survey than a genuine look at process: how a boxer-turned-novelist-turned-painter built a body of work around violence, fame, and sex without ever losing her sense of humor about it.

The show arrives with a full slate of programming — a Rachel Comey collection inspired by Drexler's work debuting at Fashion Week, a reissue of her 1974 novel The Cosmopolitan Girl, and an Anthology Film Archives program of her home movies — that together argue for Drexler as a genuinely interdisciplinary figure whose painting was only one part of a much larger creative life.

shows.title: Angelus Novus
shows.description:
Volker Hüller's third New York solo show is his first devoted purely to figuration, after a career moving fluidly between abstraction and figurative painting, collage, and sculpture. A recurring image anchors the show: a toppled stone torso, encountered again and again by different onlookers, sometimes washed ashore as a curious merman, always standing in for a fallen empire and the collapse of a political order — as relevant to the present as to antiquity.

Hüller stages these encounters in indeterminate, classically-inflected spaces — Roman columns, arched passageways — where figures range from menacing to despondent: pilgrims prostrate at an altar, men tending to another who might be sick, drunk, or dead. The show's title nods to Paul Klee's Angelus Novus and, more directly, to Walter Benjamin's reading of that painting as the "angel of history," facing the wreckage of the past while being blown backward into the future. That tension between memory, catastrophe, and forward motion runs through every canvas here.

Hüller, who studied under Norbert Schwontkowski in Hamburg, has work in the collections of MoMA and the Israel Museum; this show finds him working at a scale and clarity that push his long-standing interest in antiquity and disintegration into sharper, more explicitly narrative territory.

shows.title: die dünne Haut der Zivilisation
shows.description:
Matthias Franz's New York solo show — its title translates as "The Thin Skin of Civilization" — uses history and literary source material as a lens for the present, painting ambiguous landscapes and uncanny interiors where displaced figures drift through vast oceans or dense jungle foliage. In the die Aufklärung ("Enlightenment") paintings, cloaked figures cling to guiding lights while adrift on a yellow sea, and a levitating figure in Napoleonic uniform salutes above an archaic passenger boat — a jarring pairing of Enlightenment ideals with the militarism that so often accompanied them.

A second recurring motif, the Luddite Kids Club, pictures children gazing up at an empty, instrument-crowded bandstand — a space built for communal creation that instead holds its audience at a permanent, silent distance. Franz's reference to the 19th-century Luddite movement is deliberately not anti-technology so much as a question about the conditions and dignity under which change gets imposed on people.

Franz, who studied under Daniel Richter in Vienna, works in a lush, uncanny palette — turquoise, burnt umber, glowing yellow — that gives even his bleakest historical allegories a strange, seductive warmth.

shows.title: Queen of the Neighborhood!
shows.description:
Meghann Stephenson's third solo show borrows the architecture of Dante's Inferno to look at how morality gets gendered. Nine paintings, one for each circle of Hell, translate the classic vices — wrath, vanity, desire, heresy — into small domestic dramas: a woman disappearing into a cloud, a girl testing the edges of a picket fence, a still life apple whose rot only shows up in reflection. Rather than restaging sin as spectacle, Stephenson keeps the register quiet and interior, more about posture and self-awareness than transgression.

The work sits in a lineage of figurative painting that uses fairy tale and allegory to talk about the policing of women's behavior, but Stephenson's touch is drier and more personal than that description might suggest — closer to a diary entry than a manifesto. Having shown with galleries from Los Angeles to Hong Kong to London since her 2013 Parsons BFA, she's built a reputation for pairing sly humor with genuinely uncomfortable subject matter, and this show looks to continue that.

It's a tight, focused body of work — nine paintings built around a single conceit — which makes it a good one to see in person rather than in scattered installation shots, since the cumulative logic of the Inferno structure is part of the point.

shows.title: Cave
shows.description:
Peter Opheim's second show with The Hole is a deliberate reversal of his first. Where 2024's Cocoon was built from sunlit yellows, small-eyed clay creatures, and woven hangings, Cave goes dark and stormy: paintings rendered in layered, colorful blacks, populated by figures that read as more mysterious and more threatening than before. The ceramic works have hardened too, moving from soft clay creatures to crackled, burn-textured beings stacked on salvaged wood.

The New Mexico-based Opheim has been developing this body of imagery with The Hole since 2021, showing internationally at fairs and gallery spaces in Copenhagen, Cologne, and Tokyo. Cave asks a real question about continuity — whether these new dark-toned figures are the same cast of characters from a changed emotional weather, or an entirely new population discovered further out in the artist's imagination. Painting, ceramics, and salvaged wood construction working together in one show gives a fuller sense of Opheim's range than any single medium would.

shows.title: Savdie / Soutine
shows.description:
This is a genuinely odd and interesting pairing: a century-old École de Paris expressionist shown alongside one of the most talked-about painters of the current moment, joined by a shared conviction that instability is the actual subject of a painting, not just its style. Soutine's impasto surfaces — carcasses, portraits, and landscapes alike churned into the same feverish physicality — get read here as a direct ancestor to the way Ilana Savdie treats the body: fragmented, dressed and undressed, suspended mid-transformation, never quite settling into a single legible form.

Savdie's paintings, built from gestural marks laid over gradients and screen-inflected surfaces, have made her one of the more closely watched painters of her generation since her 2025 Creative Capital award and her Whitney Museum solo. Putting her canvases next to Soutine's 1920s carcasses and portraits is a curatorial gamble that mostly succeeds because both artists are after the same thing: color and distortion pushed until representation gives way to raw sensation.

It's a small, focused two-artist show rather than a survey, which makes the formal argument easier to follow in the gallery than it would be on paper.

shows.title: Nightcrawling
shows.description:
Oscar yi Hou's third solo show with James Fuentes moves his portrait practice out of the studio and into the club. Where his earlier paintings held sitters at a composed distance, framed by dense hand-lettered symbology, Nightcrawling dissolves that border: figures blur into drips, vapor, and washes of colored light, so that bodies and the nightlife spaces around them become a single undulating field rather than a subject against a backdrop.

Yi Hou, who had his BA from Columbia and has already shown at the Brooklyn Museum and had work acquired by the Whitney, ICA Miami, and M+, has always used portraiture to work through questions of identity and belonging — his earlier work was notably concerned with queer Chinese-American subjectivity. Here the destabilized, embedded viewpoint suggests something more experiential: the paintings are trying to capture the feeling of communal, erotic, unstructured time rather than a fixed likeness. An accompanying publication with writing from Juliana Huxtable and others extends the show's interest in nightlife as a site of collective identity.

It's a loosening-up for an artist previously known for tight, iconographic control, and worth seeing as a real formal shift rather than a variation on a theme.

shows.title: Cut the World
shows.description:
Mark Armijo McKnight works in black-and-white photography that treats bodies and desert landscape as the same kind of material — bodies photographed like rock formations, rock formations that read like skin. His pictures tend to isolate fragments (a fold, a crevice, a shadowed opening) so that scale and subject become ambiguous, and the show's title, borrowed from a Jung letter about working through depression by turning directly into its "core and ground," points to the same logic of confrontation rather than avoidance.

McKnight, who has exhibited widely on the West Coast and had work included in institutional surveys of queer photography, brings a formal rigor and a tactile, almost sculptural sensibility to a medium that easily slides into either straight documentation or overt eroticism; his best pictures sit deliberately between those modes. This is his exhibition at Klaus von Nichtssagend's Franklin Street space, continuing a body of work built around the desert Southwest and the body as terrain.

Given how much of McKnight's work depends on close, high-contrast printing, this is very much a show to see on the wall rather than on a screen.

shows.title: Keep On Truckin'
shows.description:
Michael Brown, a tattoo artist by trade turned sculptor and painter, uses this nearly two-decade survey to trace a body of work built from pop iconography, appropriated counterculture symbols, and hard, industrial materials. Three new oil-stick paintings of a cartoon middle finger anchor the show — brash, cartoonish, and rendered with the loose, immediate line of drawing rather than the built-up surface of paint.

Alongside them, Brown's "Oxidation Paintings" take mud and dirt left outdoors to weather, then trace the resulting patterns in 24-karat gold leaf, an explicit rebuttal to Warhol's own Oxidation series and a wry comment on what materials get treated as sacred. Earlier pieces round out the show: stainless-steel "cracked mirror" sculptures that replicate shattered glass, melted-vinyl-record objects that ask what culture we're made of, and a set of gleaming Budweiser cans that needle Jeff Koons's brand of high-gloss appropriation.

Taken together, the exhibition circles a consistent set of ideas — commodity, ritual, and self-deprecating humor — pop instinct filtered through a sculptor's hand.

shows.title: Tony Cragg
shows.description:
Tony Cragg has spent more than fifty years arguing that sculpture's job is to invent forms the world hasn't produced on its own — a position this show, the gallery's first solo presentation of the British sculptor in its Tribeca space, makes with real conviction. New work in bronze, wood, stone, and steel fills the gallery across three floors, ranging from the frontal, orbital form of Versus at the entrance to the large Corten-steel pieces Path and Up and Down on the ground floor, whose swelling, cascading profiles read at once as waterfall, road, and geological event.

Cragg's long-running interest in stacking and stratification shows up in a large wooden Stack and in In No Time, where inclined, conjoined columns collide into a single baroque, metamorphic mass. Upstairs, the Symmetries series — figures generated by mirroring axial line drawings — produces uncannily anatomical forms without ever setting out to depict the body, while a group of Masks, cast from sliding Janus-head profiles, layer two faces into disquieting composite portraits.

What holds the show together isn't a single material or theme but Cragg's persistent refusal of "the generic dullness" of designed, geometric form — his words — in favor of shapes arrived at through carving, casting, and accumulation. For anyone who knows Cragg mainly through museum surveys, this is a chance to see a full cross-section of his current studio output in one room.

shows.title: Notes on What is What
shows.description:
Edith Dekyndt's first solo show with the gallery takes the idea of the island — as both a literal place and a philosophical model of contained, interdependent life — as its organizing thread, drawing on Aldous Huxley's 1962 novel Island as a loose point of departure. The work grew out of two very different insular sites: Fogo Island off Newfoundland, where Dekyndt was an artist-in-residence, and Ibiza, whose long history as a magnet for outsiders and subcultures interests her for very different reasons.

Fishing ropes from Fogo fused with glass sit in vitrines alongside 3D prints on found wood and animal skins; a large tapestry, The Water Sizzling at the Prow, derives from facsimiles of boat carpets found on the island. From Ibiza comes Animal Methods, a video work built around the sloughed skin of a snake caught in the wind like a flag, and a fabric piece that spent months buried underground, absorbing the site's own slow chemistry.

Dekyndt has built a career out of letting humble materials undergo real physical change — decay, erosion, submersion — as a way of making the ecological and cultural forces around us newly visible. This show, connecting the North Atlantic to the Mediterranean, is less about representing either place than about surfacing the quieter processes, material and historical, that run beneath both.

shows.title: In Between
shows.description:
Vojtěch Kovařík paints figures that look carved rather than drawn — a legacy of his training in ceramics and sculpture, which shows up here in monumental canvases where sand-thickened paint and heavy shadow give simplified bodies real physical mass. In Between gathers large-scale mythological paintings alongside smaller "chamber" pictures and two terracotta reliefs, all built from a personal vocabulary of Greek and Roman antiquity filtered through the blocky, frontal poses of Socialist Realist monuments and the fractured bodies of Picasso's classical period.

The show's title comes from a distinction the Czech painter draws from Claude Lévi-Strauss: the bricoleur, who works with a fixed stock of secondhand materials never designed for the job at hand, versus the engineer, who starts from a blank slate. Kovařík places himself between the two, borrowing freely from friezes, war memorials, and votive statues without committing to any single tradition's meaning.

Paintings like Aglauros, Herse and Pandrosos and Between Two Worlds monumentalize touch and distance between figures, while the terracotta reliefs — including The One Who Thinks Before and The One Who Thinks After — return to the oldest of his materials, clay, worked directly by hand. It's a show about how myth functions as raw material rather than fixed narrative, and about intimacy rendered at a scale usually reserved for public monuments.

shows.title: Line Call
shows.description:
Eileen Quinlan's eighth solo show at the gallery is built around memory as an unruly, unreliable archivist. Photographs spanning twenty years of her practice are pulled back into circulation and set alongside brand-new work, including snapshot images of friends, family, and domestic space that Quinlan is showing largely untouched — a striking departure for an artist best known for heavily processed, studio-manipulated photographs that foreground instability, decay, and material change over documentary fidelity.

The show's title points to the recurring formal device holding the work together: the line, which shows up variously as a contour mapping an image's edge, an incidental mark, or a pointer directing attention outside the frame itself. In her newest works, printed on mirrored surfaces with imagery that spills past its own borders, that line becomes actively insubordinate — refusing containment the way the photographs themselves refuse a single, settled meaning.

Quinlan has spent two decades treating photography's promise to "capture and preserve" as a premise worth interrogating rather than accepting, and this survey-like show, mixing raw personal ephemera with her more constructed images, makes that tension unusually visible.

shows.title: 10 Year Anniversary
shows.description:
Magenta Plains marks a decade on the Lower East Side with a group show pulling together artists from across its exhibition history — a program that has moved fluidly between painting, sculpture, and film since the gallery's founding by Olivia Smith, Chris Dorland, and David Deutsch. Rather than a single thematic thread, expect a survey-style hang built to reflect the range and continuity of the gallery's roster over the past ten years, from longtime painters to more recent additions to the program.

Anniversary shows like this one function as a kind of self-portrait: less about any single artist's argument than about what a decade of curatorial choices adds up to when placed in one room. For regular visitors to the gallery, it's an opportunity to see familiar names in new company; for newcomers, it's as good an introduction as any to what Magenta Plains has stood for since 2016.

shows.title: Things Continue Anyway
shows.description:
Peter Barrickman's paintings work by transformation rather than description: a line that starts as a branch drifts into a ribbon, then a current, then a map; a leaf collapses into a brushstroke; a hedge becomes a cartographic survey. Things Continue Anyway gathers recent canvases where recognizable material — water, plants, windows, boats, folded paper — is layered, scraped, and revised until it settles into a state the accompanying essay by Michelle Grabner ties to Sylvia Plath's poem "Flute Notes from a Reedy Pond": not an ending, but a kind of held latency.

The largest work, Testaccio Video, depicts an illuminated apartment façade populated by smaller pictures-within-the-picture — an image that plays directly against Laura Owens's own picture-within-a-picture experiments, though where Owens catalogs and indexes painting's history, Barrickman's embedded fragments feel more like half-remembered residue drifting in from elsewhere in his own work.

What makes the paintings hold together despite that constant flux is a consistent notational logic — repeated shapes, intervals, and interruptions that behave more like a private shorthand than a fixed vocabulary. It's a show for viewers who like paintings that resist quick reading, where recognition arrives and then deliberately slips away again.

shows.title: fluorochiaroscuro
shows.description:
Michael Wilkinson's first show with the gallery updates still-life painting for an age of ambient screen light. He photographs cut flowers, cherry blossom branches, and solitary fruit set against tightly stretched, unpainted linen, then paints from those source images so that blank canvas and painted illusion occupy the same surface — the linen functions simultaneously as the ground and as its own depicted subject, all held within matching thin aluminum frames.

The technique he calls "fluorochiaroscuro" pushes traditional light-and-shadow modeling further by working in fluorescent pigment, intensifying the effect of light hitting each subject until ordinary objects start to look faintly otherworldly. Paintings like the Delphinium series track a single flower across a day, shadows lengthening and dissolving into abstraction as the light shifts — a fascination Wilkinson traces back to the enforced slowness of pandemic lockdown, when domestic objects became newly worth close attention.

The result sits somewhere between trompe l'oeil illusionism and conceptual art's interest in the readymade, using a genre as old as painting itself to think about time, transience, and the strange charge of paying very close attention to very ordinary things.

shows.title: The Wanderers
shows.description:
Hew Locke's third solo show with the gallery continues his decades-long project of tracing empire's afterlives through objects that carry, quite literally, the weight of history. The centerpiece is a new fleet in his ongoing Odyssey series — intricately embellished votive boats modeled on the devotional ships once hung in churches as offerings for safe passage, here ranging from seventeenth-century galleons to twentieth-century tankers, each one laden with beads, medals, cowrie shells, coins, and imagery lifted from Locke's own altered share certificates.

Elsewhere, Locke's Souvenirs take nineteenth-century Parian ware busts of Queen Victoria, Horatio Nelson, and George Washington and dress them in found materials mimicking precious metal and ceremonial regalia, turning commemorative Victorian objects into carnival figures "weighed down," in the artist's words, "by the literal burden of history." A new sculpture, Foreign Exchange 3, reimagines a Victoria monument overtaken by Caribbean vernacular architecture and tropical color, extending Locke's long-running interest in what happens to public monuments once they're forced into dialogue with the places and peoples they once claimed to represent.

Two new series debut alongside these — Knight Errant, watercolors reimagining Arthurian legend through Locke's own colonial-era Guyanese schooling, and Spirit House, watercolors of Guyanese timber houses populated by memento mori figures — rounding out a show that treats migration, trade, and colonial commerce as a continuous, still-unfolding story rather than settled history.

shows.title: Baby Mozart's Kiss
shows.description:
Kelsey Isaacs returns to Theta for her second solo show at the gallery, following her 2023 debut there. Isaacs builds her paintings from photographs of scenes she stages and lights herself, then translates them into oil on linen and, notably, oil on aluminum panel - a support that gives her images a hard, almost lacquered surface quality that pushes against their otherwise soft, cinematic staging.

The title work, Cupid, is characteristic of her method: a tightly cropped, theatrically lit image that sits somewhere between illustration, film still, and religious painting, rendered with a glossy technical control that makes its artifice both obvious and seductive. Isaacs has described her own interest in staged tableaux that read as intimate even as their construction is fully visible, and that tension between sincerity and performance runs through her recent gallery and art-fair presentations, including a solo booth at Art Basel Miami Beach.

Coming off a strong run of institutional attention - her work has shown alongside a roster of Theta artists at the gallery's group exhibitions and in a Frieze London solo presentation - this show is a chance to see a fuller body of new paintings by an artist whose combination of technical facility and image-making intelligence has made her one of the gallery's most closely watched names.

hours: Mon - Fri 12pm to 6pm, or by appointment

shows.title: Land animal, house animal
shows.description:
Tanya Merrill's third solo show at 303 continues her project of turning close observation of the natural world into quietly charged domestic scenes. Painted largely at her studio in the Hudson Valley, the new canvases fold a marsh hawk gliding over open fields, a loose horse at night, and a cat curling into bedsheets together with intimate images of new motherhood and partnership — the show follows closely on the birth of the artist's child, and that experience runs through the work as a kind of hinge between animal instinct and domestic life.

Merrill paints with oil thinned almost to the consistency of watercolor, and graphite, chasing the fluid, on-the-spot feel of a sketchbook made outdoors. The result is a body of work that moves fluidly between plein-air looking and staged, symbolic tableaux, populated by a recurring cast — hawks, horses, columbine, cats — that function almost like family members. Historical art-historical references and American folk imagery surface throughout, giving the paintings a layered, almost narrative quality even when a single canvas depicts nothing more than a flower bending in shade.

It's a show about the strange, permeable border between household and habitat, human and animal — appropriate territory for an artist whose whole practice lives in that overlap. Concurrently on view in the gallery's Project Room is new watercolor work by Tim Gardner.

shows.title: The World Tangled in You
shows.description:
This is Maia Cruz Palileo's first New York presentation with David Kordansky, and it arrives as a fully realized statement of a two-decade project: reworking archival photographs of the Philippine-American War and family history into paintings that are as much about the physical act of painting as they are about historical reckoning. Palileo builds compositions from collaged and repeated fragments of found photographs, so that soldiers, landscapes, and figures recur and mutate across a canvas rather than settling into a single legible narrative.

The large-scale paintings pull from Palileo's research in the Philippine archives at Chicago's Newberry Library — one pivotal work reveals a field of marching soldiers that, viewed as a whole, resolves into an X, an image the artist has likened to a record skipping, where history gets stuck and repeats. Smaller, more intuitive paintings elsewhere in the show work more directly from the photographic source, without the collage-based interventions, giving a fuller sense of the range in Palileo's practice between research-driven and purely embodied ways of working. Color itself carries history in this work too — khaki tones nod to 1946, the year of Philippine independence, while other palettes echo the incongruous uniforms of American soldiers.

It's an ambitious gallery debut: paintings that use the pleasure of paint-handling as a way of inhabiting family and national trauma without flattening it into illustration. For anyone who followed Palileo's museum surveys over the past few years, this is the first chance to see how that research has matured into large-scale New York gallery presentation.

shows.title: Silent Night
shows.description:
Scott Kahn has spent more than fifty years painting a version of representational landscape that sits just slightly out of true — skies that curdle into unnatural color, windows that open onto scenes that feel more remembered than observed. This show at Zwirner's 20th Street space gathers new and recent paintings alongside work spanning the last twenty-five years, tracing the landscape motifs — moonlit fields, bare trees, picture windows — that have anchored his practice since the 1970s.

What distinguishes Kahn's landscapes is their double register: they read at first as fairly straightforward depictions of a place — a backyard, a stand of trees, a night sky — but the color and light are pitched to feel uncanny, almost hallucinatory, without ever tipping into outright surrealism. A cloud might glow with an internal light no real cloud has; a moonscape might feel more ominous than any actual night walk. Kahn's commitment to a consistent, almost obsessive way of looking at the ordinary over five decades gives the show real weight — this isn't a survey of stylistic evolution so much as a demonstration of how much can be mined from returning again and again to the same handful of motifs.

Coming to wider market attention only in the last several years despite a career dating to the 1970s, Kahn has become one of the more quietly influential painters of atmospheric, semi-surreal landscape for a younger generation of realists. This is a rare chance to see the arc of that work assembled in one place.

shows.title: A Logo for America
shows.description:
In April 1987, Alfredo Jaar — five years after arriving in New York from Chile — hijacked the Spectacolor billboard in Times Square for a Public Art Fund commission and ran a brief, blunt animation: the phrase "This Is Not America" overlaid on a map of the United States, followed by the outline of the whole continent and the words "America" reclaimed for the hemisphere it actually names. Nearly forty years later, and amid the U.S. semiquincentennial, Galerie Lelong devotes a full exhibition to unpacking the piece's origins and afterlife.

The show centers a newly digitized version of the original animation, projected at scale in a darkened room, shown alongside the original storyboard drawings — exhibited publicly for the first time — that reveal how tightly Jaar plotted the piece's rhetorical structure. Around that core, photographic suites, lightboxes, and videos trace the work's subsequent lives: restagings on a barge off Miami Beach, on television screens, in other cities and other contexts, each iteration adjusting the piece's confrontation with what "American" is assumed to mean.

It's a rare opportunity to see a landmark of public-art conceptualism dismantled and reassembled as gallery exhibition — less a retrospective than an anatomy of how one three-word provocation has kept finding new relevance for four decades.

shows.title: Sugar on My Tongue
shows.description:
Marc Dennis paints like an Old Master and thinks like a stand-up comic. His second solo show at Harper's is a room of hyperrealist still lifes that borrow the gravity of Dutch Golden Age vanitas painting — glossy fruit, gleaming silver, dying flowers — and then puncture it with images pulled from consumer culture: cheerleaders, penguins, iridescent bubbles, a stray reference to Jeff Koons's "Rabbit" propped next to a muted floral arrangement.

The paintings work because Dennis doesn't skimp on the craft that makes the joke land — every reflection and glaze is rendered with the kind of patience associated with 17th-century painting, which is exactly what lets the campier images borrow real pictorial authority. The effect is somewhere between a memento mori and a punchline, and it's very much about the pleasure of looking itself: surfaces built to seduce the eye before the content registers.

It's a good show for anyone who likes their art history with a sense of humor, and a chance to see how far a painter can stretch a genre without breaking its rules. Dennis, who lives and works in New York, has spent the last few years refining this exact collision of vanitas and pop kitsch, and this batch of new paintings feels like some of his most confident yet.

shows.title: The Office of Inter-American Affairs Presents
shows.description:
Ana Segovia's first solo show at kurimanzutto's New York space digs into the gaucho, the Southern Cone's answer to the American cowboy, and pulls it apart as a piece of manufactured national mythology. The paintings are big and vividly colored but deliberately incomplete: a hat, a poncho, a pair of wide-legged trousers, a hand around a mate gourd, each cropped tight like a film still that withholds the rest of the picture.

That cinematic framing isn't incidental — Segovia builds the show around archival footage from the real-life Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs, the U.S. propaganda outfit that spent the 1940s exporting a flattering image of Pan-American unity while quietly extending U.S. influence across Latin America. Two monitors run OCIAA footage of Uruguay and Chile, and a related video work isolates dancers' legs and feet in gaucho trousers, denying the viewer a full body to look at. A suite of charcoal storyboards and a pair of pastel-toned landscape paintings, indebted to Uruguayan planismo and the painter Petrona Viera, round out the installation.

It's a smart, formally rigorous show about how images make identity — how a costume, a camera angle, and decades of repetition can turn a working horseman into a symbol of masculinity and nationhood. Segovia treats painting itself as another kind of edit, cropping and recoloring found footage until the constructedness of the myth becomes the actual subject.

shows.title: Rana Begum
shows.description:
Rana Begum's first New York solo show is built around light as both subject and material. The centerpiece is a suspended sculpture from her Chainlink series, in which ordinary chain-link fencing is rewoven into a soft, textured cloud-like form — an industrial material stripped of its usual menace and turned into something closer to a Rothko-inflected color field.

Around it are works from her Louvre series, which take the humble architectural louvre — the slatted panels found in blinds, façades and vents — and rebuild them in metal, stone, and glass to explore how different materials bend and hold light. A newer Fold series, inspired partly by Bangladeshi kite-making, turns flat sheet metal into precisely creased wall reliefs whose folds throw shifting shadows and unexpected color onto the surrounding wall.

Begum, who was born in Bangladesh and trained at Chelsea College of Art and the Slade, works in a lineage that runs from Agnes Martin and Donald Judd through the geometric traditions of Islamic art and architecture, and this show is a good primer on how she braids those references into a quietly meditative, repetition-based practice. It's abstraction you're meant to walk around, not just look at — the works genuinely change as your position and the light in the room shifts.

shows.title: House Rules
shows.description:
Anna Park draws in charcoal at a scale and speed that reads more like action painting than illustration, and "House Rules" turns that jittery, black-and-white mark-making loose on the imagery of casinos, carnival games, and Las Vegas. Slot machines, dice, prize claws and midway barkers dissolve into tangles of gestural lines, limbs, and half-legible signage, with figures emerging and disappearing inside the compositional chaos.

Park, who was born in South Korea and grew up in Utah, has talked about her outsider's vantage on American culture, and this body of work uses the vocabulary of games — winning, losing, "the house always wins" — as a stand-in for bigger ideas about competition, risk, and the mythology of the American Dream. Titles like "Lucky You" and "Try Me" have a carnival-barker knowingness that undercuts the glamour of the imagery even as the drawings revel in it.

It's a good showcase for Park's central trick: building recognizable scenes almost entirely out of speed and gesture, so that a composition only resolves into legibility the longer you look. The show rewards that kind of looking, and it's a strong example of how she's pushed the black-and-white charcoal drawing into genuinely large, ambitious wall-filling compositions.

shows.title: A Burnt Child Loves the Fire
shows.description:
Dora Jeridi's debut at Marianne Boesky is a set of large, theatrical paintings that stage plush, half-remembered domestic interiors — leather sofas, dining sets, ornately framed portraits loosely drawn from her grandmother's Parisian apartment — and then let them come apart. Sweeping drapery in purple, gold, and red floods across the furniture like a geological event, and passages of oily black cross-hatching eat into the scenes from the edges.

Jeridi, who is French but has lived in New York for the past few years, spent time in the Dior archive researching historic garments from the Galliano era, and that research shows up as an interest in drapery as both a symbol of luxury and a purely abstract, expressive device — a tradition she traces back through the history of painting. A Picasso "Guernica" quotation surfaces amid the domestic wreckage, a reminder that beauty and violence have always shared the same canvas in her work.

The show's title comes from Oscar Wilde's inversion of an old proverb, and that inversion is the engine of the whole body of work: comfort and catastrophe, elegance and darkness, pulling on each other in the same frame. It's an ambitious, confident first outing for a painter still early in her career.

shows.title: Mathemagical
shows.description:
The Haas Brothers, twins Nikolai and Simon, build their sculptures and paintings by hand-applying mathematical rules the way you'd follow a recipe: start with a simple form, then add material — paint, clay, wax, glass beads — according to a fixed algorithm, and watch a complex pattern emerge. It's the same logic that governs coral growth, cave formations, and the spots on animal fur, and their fourth solo show with the gallery pushes that method to its most elaborate scale yet.

The biggest object in the room, "Peach Tree," folds together nearly every technique in their toolkit: a carved stone base honoring their stonemason father, a bronze trunk textured with their signature "Accretion" wax-building process, and glass-bead foliage hand-made by the Haas Sisters, a group of women from a farming community in central California who've spent years learning the brothers' particular beading algorithm. New "Accretion" paintings take nostalgic landscape scenes and abstract them almost past recognition by applying paint according to a reaction-diffusion equation — the same math that describes how animal markings form.

The show runs alongside "Uncanny Valley," the duo's traveling mid-career survey opening this fall at the Blanton Museum of Art, so it's a good moment to see how their oddball, rigorously systematic sense of humor has scaled up from tabletop objects to room-filling sculpture without losing its warmth.

shows.title: Gary Hume
shows.description:
Gary Hume returns to Matthew Marks with twenty new paintings in his signature household enamel on aluminum, installed against a hand-painted mural that the artist made specifically for the gallery's walls. The mural, drawn in acrylic and charcoal, recreates cartoon murals that once decorated a UK immigration center for asylum seekers before officials had them painted over in 2023 for being "too welcoming" — turning a bureaucratic erasure into the backdrop for new work.

The paintings themselves stay close to Hume's long-running vocabulary: intertwined swans, flowers, and abstracted female forms rendered in his glossy, high-key enamel, alongside new imagery pulled from the murals. Hume has always worked at the edge between legibility and pure surface, and this pairing of slick panel paintings with a raw, drawn wall makes that tension unusually explicit.

It's a good chance to see a British Pop-adjacent painter, long associated with the YBA generation, pushing his flat, sign-like imagery into more overtly political territory without losing the deadpan wit that has defined his work since the 1990s.

shows.title: Space Remembers
shows.description:
Leidy Churchman's second Matthew Marks show gathers fifteen new paintings, anchored by five large-scale canvases (six by nine feet) that treat the picture plane as a kind of gravitational field for home, memory, and belief. One painting places Churchman's own house on an island off the coast of Maine in an unruly tableau — a cow with a blueberry bush sprouting from its side, two lobsters, a Buddhist protector deity floating overhead — while another opens a storm drain into the swirling chambers of a nautilus shell, mirrored across the room by a portal-like lotus flower.

Churchman has always worked promiscuously across subject matter, pulling from nature, internet ephemera, and religious iconography with the same flat, deceptively casual touch. Here that method sharpens into something more ritualized: in Center of the Universe (Ratna), the artist renders their own body in pieces, a direct reference to the Tibetan Buddhist practice of chöd, in which a practitioner visualizes offering their body to sustain other beings, human and not.

The paintings ask to be read less as landscapes than as maps of consciousness — an ongoing inquiry, in Churchman's words, into what can be known and how. It's an ambitious, image-hungry show from an artist whose reach across scale and subject keeps expanding.

shows.title: Jumping Jive
shows.description:
Michael Rosenfeld reopens for the fall with a show devoted to Norman Lewis (1909–1979), the pioneering Black abstract expressionist whose rhythmic, calligraphic canvases drew directly on jazz and the improvisational energy of Harlem nightlife. "Jumping Jive" — its title borrowed from the Cab Calloway standard — foregrounds that musical undercurrent in Lewis's work, tracing how the syncopation and gesture of swing and bebop fed into his all-over compositions of small marks and figures in motion.

Lewis spent decades navigating the space between abstraction and social content, a founding member of Spiral and one of the few Black artists embraced by the Abstract Expressionist circle even as his work was long overlooked by the market and museums built around that movement. This gallery has done more than almost any other space to correct that record, and a show keyed to Lewis's engagement with music offers a different entry point into a body of work usually discussed in terms of politics or formal innovation alone.

Expect dense fields of gestural marks that read, depending on distance, as abstract pattern or as crowds of dancing figures — a hallmark of Lewis's ability to hold multiple readings in suspension within a single canvas.

shows.title: Fitting
shows.description:
For her tenth solo show with Miles McEnery, Suzanne Caporael turns the four-color theorem of cartography — the principle that any map can be colored with just four hues so that no two adjacent regions match — into a working method for painting. Polyomino shapes (the blocky, interlocking forms familiar from Tetris) tessellate across each canvas, their edges softened by Caporael's layered, semi-opaque handling of oil on linen so that a rigid mathematical system ends up looking almost weather-worn.

Caporael has spent decades making abstraction that quietly borrows structure from outside art — statistics, geology, color theory — and then lets paint handling undo the rigidity of the source. The polyomino paintings continue that logic: a closed combinatorial system rendered permeable by the surface itself, so the "proof" the works construct is felt more than read.

It's a cerebral premise carried by a genuinely sensuous surface, and worth seeing for the way Caporael's touch keeps a game-like structure from ever feeling merely diagrammatic.

shows.title: Evidence to the Contrary
shows.description:
Roy Dowell presents twenty-five small, uniformly sized panels (all 24 by 18 inches) built from vinyl emulsion on linen, a medium he favors because it keeps every layer of the painting's history visible rather than burying earlier decisions under later ones. The works read like an inventory of a private cabinet of curiosities — fragments of pattern, found form, and personal reference accumulated across a career split between Los Angeles and Mexico City.

Dowell has long made a virtue of self-quotation, treating his own back catalog as raw material rather than something to be avoided, and here that habit becomes explicit: motifs recur and mutate from panel to panel, less a survey than a working notebook. He's said he prefers not to over-determine meaning for the viewer, opting instead for a kind of open invitation to decode each composition on its own terms.

Taken together the twenty-five works function like a single expanded painting, each panel a discrete unit of the same restless visual language, and the show rewards the kind of slow, panel-by-panel looking its scale invites.

shows.title: The Language of Flowers
shows.description:
Isca Greenfield-Sanders turns to floral painting for her fifth solo show at Miles McEnery, but with a process that departs from her earlier found-photograph-based work: every reference image here is her own, shot on visits to gardens at home and abroad. Each painting begins as a watercolor, which is enlarged, printed, and mounted to canvas before Greenfield-Sanders builds up a full acrylic painting on top of it — a layered method that lets a fast, loose watercolor gesture coexist with a much slower painted surface.

The historical touchstones are specifically women who painted flowers — Clara Peeters, Mary Delany, Agnes Northrop — a lineage Greenfield-Sanders places herself in deliberately rather than incidentally. The resulting canvases sit somewhere between botanical illustration and hazy, atmospheric memory, less interested in taxonomic precision than in the sensation of a fleeting encounter with a bloom.

It's a tightly focused show, formally inventive in its combination of print and paint, and a good look at an artist reworking her signature process around a new, more intimate subject.

shows.title: Beautiful, Perfect Things
shows.description:
Lucy Williams makes her gallery debut with Miles McEnery through intricate mixed-media collages that reconstruct architectural interiors — bookcases, modernist rooms, threaded assemblages — out of cut paper, Perspex, and engineered wood. Her scenes hover between built-up realism and abstraction, drawing heavily on British modernism and Bauhaus design, and each component is sourced with enough specificity that the collages read as much as constructed archives as pictures.

Williams works slowly and materially: color studies, woven textile tests, and swatch experiments precede each finished piece, and the works are conceived as being in conversation with one another, echoing forms and palettes across the show. That deliberateness sits alongside a real sense of play, with unexpected juxtapositions of pattern and texture keeping the meticulous compositions from tipping into mere precision.

As an inaugural solo outing, the show is a strong introduction to an artist whose collage-built rooms reward close, patient looking — the kind of work where the pleasure is in noticing how each fragment was chosen.

shows.title: The Ultimate Works
shows.description:
Curated by Luis Pérez-Oramas, this show bookends the long career of Tomie Ohtake (1913–2015) by pairing her late, nearly monochrome white paintings and sculptures with the "blind paintings" she made between 1960 and 1963, when she worked with her eyes covered at the suggestion of critic Mário Pedrosa. The exhibition's premise is that these two extremes — the enforced darkness of the blindfold and the near-total whiteness of her final canvases — are connected poles of the same lifelong investigation into perception and intuition.

Ohtake, who moved from Kyoto to Brazil in 1936 and didn't begin painting until her late thirties, spent decades developing a language of organic forms and subtle tonal gradation that eventually extended into large-scale sculpture and public commissions. The white paintings on view here build up thick, sculptural layers of paint that catch light and cast shadow across their own surface, while tubular white steel sculptures carry that same gestural, looping movement into three dimensions.

It's a rare chance in New York to see the late work of one of Brazil's most significant abstract painters, staged specifically to draw out the arc between her earliest experiments and her final, most reductive statements.

shows.title: Seeing in Blue
shows.description:
Torkwase Dyson's new paintings grow out of more than a decade of scuba and free diving, translating what she calls the "boundless state change of water" into atmospheric washes layered beneath her signature curvilinear, engineered forms. Dyson begins each canvas on the floor, pooling translucent color before building up geometric constructions in shaped wooden panels, string, and hardware — a working method that stages a tension between chance-based mark-making and deliberate construction.

Where her earlier work often ran dark, Seeing in Blue foregrounds aquatic tones: in Interbeing Blue, titanium white pushes the blues toward incandescence, cut by flickers of dark green and rust-red. Dyson has spent her career thinking through black geography, ecology, and infrastructure at architectural scale, and these paintings compress that research into an intimate register — less about depicting the underwater world than about replicating the embodied experience of perceiving it, the pressure and buoyancy of a body suspended in water.

The show arrives alongside a striking run of institutional recognition, including Dyson's animation debut at the Carnegie International and a large-scale installation in the current Venice Biennale, making this a good moment to see how that expanded practice folds back into paint.

shows.title: She Said She Said
shows.description:
Arlene Shechet's first New York show with Pace since 2020 pairs monumental metal sculpture with intimately scaled ceramics, extending the momentum of her acclaimed 2024 Storm King presentation "Girl Group" into new aluminum and Cor-Ten steel works. The large pieces fold and cut sheet metal into organic, biomorphic volumes that open onto pockets of空间 — sorry, of open space — leaving welds, seams, and cuts visibly part of the finished form rather than smoothed away.

The ceramic works, grouped as Touching Ground, revive terra sigillata, an ancient burnishing technique used on Greek and Roman tableware, giving the clay a luminous, glaze-free sheen in reds, blacks, and oranges. Shechet has spent years pushing clay's status as a "craft" material into ambitious, large-scale sculptural territory, and pairing it here with heavy industrial metal makes the throughline in her process — construction, revision, and improvisation across radically different materials — unusually legible.

Handmade aluminum folding chairs scattered through the installation extend Shechet's ongoing interest in seating as part of the exhibition experience, an invitation to slow down inside work that rewards a longer look.

shows.title: KNOTTING, TYING, FOLDING
shows.description:
Spanning more than five decades of Lynda Benglis's sculpture, this show moves from Sparkle Knot IV (1972) — a plaster- and glitter-covered knot of wire mesh that helped launch her lifelong interest in knotting and twisting form — through gold-leafed pleated wall reliefs of the 1980s, sand-cast glass works from 1985, folded ceramics from the 2010s, and recent bronze and paper sculptures. Benglis emerged out of Postminimalism by refusing its restraint, embracing color, glitter, and frankly sensuous surfaces at a moment when severity was the dominant mode.

The show's throughline is process made visible: pleated wire mesh covered in plaster and metal, molten glass bent and knotted by hand, chicken wire skinned in painted handmade paper. Across every material, Benglis treats surface and structure as inseparable — "the light, and the change of light, was a goal," as she has put it about the pleated works — turning what could be purely decorative gestures into serious formal inquiry.

With a Kunstmuseum Basel retrospective and a Tate Modern showing on the horizon, this survey-in-miniature is a useful primer on an artist whose restless material experimentation has never really stopped evolving.

shows.title: You Red The Shirt Off My Back
shows.description:
Eric N. Mack debuts new free-standing and wall-based work at Paula Cooper's 534 West 21st Street space, continuing his practice of building paintings out of draped and stretched fabric rather than canvas alone. Works like A truer before / Cape hang stainless steel armatures with sheets of dyed and found textile, letting the material's own drape, sheen, and prior life do much of the compositional work — sculpture and painting collapsed into a single gesture.

Mack has built a reputation on this kind of material intelligence, treating fabric as a carrier of history and reference (fashion, domestic textiles, art history) rather than a neutral support, and this show follows recent solo presentations at the American Academy of Arts and Letters and the Wexner Center for the Arts. The title's play on "you read the shirt off my back" hints at the show's interest in clothing, exposure, and vulnerability as much as pure formal invention.

It's a chance to see an artist who has become one of the more distinctive voices in draped-textile painting pushing further into freestanding, architectural forms.

shows.title: Zephyr, Zephyr
shows.description:
Tauba Auerbach brings together a family of new work across media for Zephyr, Zephyr, including paintings from an ongoing Foam series alongside moving sculpture and sound — a combination that reflects Auerbach's longstanding interest in treating painting, structure, and physical phenomena as continuous rather than separate disciplines. The title's repetition (a zephyr being a soft, gentle wind) suggests a show built around echo, oscillation, and the way a single form or motion can double back on itself.

Auerbach has spent years moving fluidly between weaving, bookbinding, glassblowing, and now kinetic sculpture and sound, always returning to questions of pattern, dimensionality, and perception — how something flat can imply depth, or how a static object can suggest motion. The addition of sound and moving parts to this exhibition marks a further expansion of that range beyond the wall-based work Auerbach is best known for.

For anyone who has followed Auerbach's shift from op-art-adjacent painting toward more physical, spatial investigations, this is a chance to see that trajectory continue into genuinely kinetic territory.

shows.title: New Openings Against Old Surfaces: On Gordon Matta-Clark's Walls Paper
shows.description:
This show is the first devoted specifically to the publishing side of Gordon Matta-Clark's practice, built around his 1973 artist's book Walls Paper. That publication gathered low-contrast black-and-white photographs of crumbling, half-demolished tenement walls across the South Bronx and Lower East Side, overprinted with hazy neon color and bound into newsprint pages split into two separate booklets — a formally strange object made at the height of the fiscal crisis and the abandonment that defined so much of New York's built environment in the early 1970s.

The exhibition traces the project back to its first public airing, a 1972 solo show at the artist-run space 112 Greene Street, where cut fragments from Matta-Clark's early building interventions (including Bronx Floors and a chunk of wall from his restaurant project FOOD) hung alongside strips of Walls Paper printed floor to ceiling. Archival material on view includes test prints, uncut printer sheets, documentary photographs, and an original set of prints from that installation, alongside material tied to his other published projects Splitting and Circus—The Caribbean Orange, plus a hand-cut unique artist's book and a recreation of the never-realized Quadrille.

Organized with the Matta-Clark estate and the artist's archive at the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and timed to Printed Matter's 50th anniversary, the show also includes two new commissions from contemporary artists responding to Matta-Clark's legacy. It's a tightly focused, archivally rich look at how one of the defining sculptors of 1970s New York used the printed page to extend his interventions into the city's crumbling fabric.

shows.title: Solid Light, 1973, 2020, 2026
shows.description:
Anthony McCall has spent more than fifty years turning projected light into something you can walk through, and this show lines up three versions of that idea side by side. The anchor is "Line Describing a Cone" (1973), the work that made his name: over half an hour, a single line of projected light slowly traces a circle, and the haze in the room resolves it into a hollow, walk-around cone of solid-seeming light. Seeing it in person rather than in documentation is the whole point — you become part of the sculpture by moving through the beam.

Alongside it are "Skylight" (2020), a vertical light cone projected downward onto a plinth and scored by composer David Grubbs with distant thunder and rain, and "Swarm" (2026), a new work making its debut here, in which two conical volumes of light rotate against each other to an escalating soundtrack. Seen together, the three pieces trace McCall's arc from analog 16mm film to fully digital, sound-driven installation without losing the basic, almost primitive experience at their core: a beam of light made physical.

This is a rare chance to see McCall's foundational film-as-sculpture alongside his most current work under one roof, useful for anyone curious how a five-decade-old avant-garde gesture still generates new pieces today.

shows.title: When the Center Holds
shows.description:
Luke Agada's first show with Sean Kelly brings together new paintings and drawings built around bodies that never quite resolve into fixed shape — figures dissolve into fragmented architecture and biomorphic form, floating in landscapes that resist any single geography. Born in Lagos and now based in Chicago, Agada paints from the vantage of someone whose sense of place has always been plural, and that shows in the way his compositions layer memory, migration, and invented topography rather than picturing any one location.

The title nods to Yeats — "the center will not hold" — but Agada flips the despair of that line into something more resilient: identity here isn't a fixed point that erodes under pressure, but something continuously reassembled through displacement. That optimism is worth noting in a body of work that otherwise traffics in fragmentation and ambiguity.

It's a strong pairing with the McCall show opening the same night in the upstairs galleries, and worth seeing for anyone tracking how younger painters are handling diasporic subject matter without falling into illustration.

shows.title: Reading the Waves
shows.description:
Sandra Vásquez de la Horra's first exhibition with Tanya Bonakdar brings her signature wax-dipped works on paper into a full architectural installation built around water and cosmology. Her drawings — figures, animals, and symbols rendered in graphite and colored pencil, then dipped in beeswax so the paper turns translucent and slightly warped — read as folk-devotional objects as much as fine art, pulling from Latin American popular imagery, indigenous healing traditions, and personal mythology.

For this show the gallery becomes something like a chapel: a circular arrangement of large-scale drawings in the main space is oriented to the cardinal points, and a suspended leporello (an accordion-fold paper sculpture) depicting the ocean deity Yemanyá hangs in the upstairs gallery in a nod to the nearby Hudson River. Recurring themes of tides, rain, and marine life run through triptychs of Olokun, the Orisha of the deep ocean, while a separate room upstairs turns toward plant life and the earth goddess Pachamama.

Vásquez de la Horra has had a strong run of institutional attention recently, including a show at Haus der Kunst in Munich, and this New York debut is a good chance to see how her intimate, almost devotional works on paper can be blown up into an immersive, room-filling environment without losing their strangeness.

shows.title: Double Vision
shows.description:
Maia Ruth Lee's second show with Tina Kim takes migration not as a subject to depict but as a way of seeing — the title borrows Homi Bhabha's idea of the migrant's simultaneous awareness of the place left and the place arrived at. The centerpiece is a new series of large paintings built from her ongoing "Bondage Baggage" motif, in which the bound, overstuffed travel bundles common to migrant labor and market trade become abstracted stacks of shape and color, turning functional luggage into a kind of glyph for displacement itself.

Around those paintings, Lee expands into sculpture and video: latex casts that preserve the imprint of bound bundles after the objects inside have been removed, a new video installation drawing on her family's home footage from Nepal and Korea, and a set of steel "glyphs" — salvaged architectural fragments from New York City reworked into an illegible, sculptural alphabet. The effect across the two gallery floors is of an archive that keeps folding and refolding itself, mirroring the way memory and inherited history don't sit still.

Lee's work has been gaining serious institutional traction — she's shown at the Whitney Biennial and has pieces in the Whitney's and Philadelphia Museum's collections — and this exhibition is a good measure of how she's translating a very personal, biographical vocabulary into increasingly ambitious physical form.

shows.title: RAGE™
shows.description:
Tania Franco Klein's debut at Yancey Richardson treats rage as the defining emotional register of the present moment — not just felt, but manufactured, packaged, and sold back to us through advertising, news media, and film. Her staged photographs borrow the visual grammar of those sources directly: cinematic lighting, advertising-style compositions, and a recurring female protagonist caught in states of tension that read as both genuinely felt and performed for an audience.

Franco Klein has built her career on psychologically loaded, highly constructed images that treat emotion as a social product rather than a private experience, and this series pushes that idea further by incorporating AI-generated imagery and manipulated subtitles alongside straight photography, blurring the line between authentic response and engineered spectacle. The trademark symbol in the title is the tell — she's naming rage as a branded commodity, not just a mood.

It's a sharp, of-the-moment body of work from an artist whose photographs already sit in major museum collections, and worth seeing alongside the concurrent Manuel Álvarez Bravo exhibition for the contrast between Franco Klein's manufactured contemporary anxiety and Bravo's quieter, older mysteries.

shows.title: Manuel Álvarez Bravo
shows.description:
This is a compact survey of one of Latin American Modernism's foundational photographers, timed to run alongside Tania Franco Klein's RAGE™ in the gallery's main space. Manuel Álvarez Bravo, largely self-taught and working in Mexico City from the 1920s onward, became known for photographs that found something unsettling or metaphorical in ordinary scenes — sleeping figures, street vendors, daydreaming women — using shadow and framing to push quiet moments toward the surreal without staging anything overtly fantastical.

The selection on view includes several of his best-known images, including "La hija de los danzantes" and "Los agachados," alongside portraits and studies that trace his relationships with Tina Modotti, Edward Weston, and the Mexican avant-garde more broadly. Bravo showed with André Breton's Surrealists in Paris and Mexico City but always kept some distance from the label, and that ambivalence is visible in the work itself — image after image that reads as documentary until you look again.

For anyone interested in the roots of Latin American photography or in how a "straight" photographic image can carry symbolic weight without obvious manipulation, this is a rare chance to see a tight grouping of vintage prints from a photographer who shaped the medium's development in the region.
